extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and educators interested in explanation in proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Apply Steiner's account to judge whether a mathematical proof explains (why) rather than merely verifies (that). Focuses on identifying characterizing properties and using the deformation test to assess generalizability and explanatory depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing property (core criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Makes critical use of some characterizing property" — a property unique to the entity in question within its domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof works because of what makes the object what it is, not because of accidental features. Identify the 'load-bearing' property the proof uses; if the proof exploits that property essentially, it is explanatory in Steiner's sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deformation test (operational criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Vary the characterizing property in the proof. The proof should yield a corresponding theorem under the deformation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If changing the characterizing property produces a family of related theorems via the same proof pattern, the original proof is explanatory. If the proof fails under deformation, it is accidental. Use the test as a concrete check of whether the proof identifies what's responsible for the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for applying the deformation test
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a proof P of theorem T: identify the property P uses critically; substitute a related property; check whether the proof goes through with corresponding modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise: (1) Identify the critical property without which P fails. (2) Substitute a related property (e.g., different symmetry/invariant). (3) Attempt to carry the proof through with the modification. (4) If it succeeds, mark explanatory; if it fails, mark non-explanatory. The page lists these five procedural steps as an operational method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner condition 1: dependence on a characterizing property
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is explanatory iff it depends on a characterizing property of the entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dependence must be non-accidental: the argument should make essential use of a property that picks out the object within its domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner condition 2: variations in property yield variations in conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations in that property yield variations in the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If modifying the characterizing property leads naturally to a modified theorem (rather than breaking the argument altogether), the proof displays explanatory generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner condition 3: proof exhibits variations as a natural family
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof exhibits these variations as a natural family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof should present or at least admit a natural family of related arguments/results parameterized by the characterizing property, showing that the result is part of a systematic pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-explanatory markers (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is non-explanatory if it: uses generic machinery (induction, term-by-term verification, brute-force calculation); cannot be deformed into proofs of related theorems; yields the result without revealing what about the entity caused it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an inductive proof that only verifies the nth case without revealing underlying structure; a computation that produces the result but doesn't appeal to properties distinguishing the object. Such proofs verify but do not explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as a characterizing property: mathematically intrinsic
rubrics_metrics.description: The property should be mathematically intrinsic: part of the object's essential nature within its domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer properties that are intrinsic to the mathematical object (e.g., symmetry of an arithmetic progression, topological features of a disk), not accidental or externally imposed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as a characterizing property: distinguishing
rubrics_metrics.description: The property should be distinguishing: it picks the object out from others in the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A characterizing property should single out the object (or class) so that the proof's reliance on it explains why this object, rather than others, has the property in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as a characterizing property: generalizable
rubrics_metrics.description: The property should be generalizable: it admits natural variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizing properties should permit systematic deformation; if you can vary the property and obtain corresponding theorems, the property counts as explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied rubric: identify and test the load-bearing property
rubrics_metrics.description: For each proof: identify the proof's load-bearing property; vary that property — does the proof generalize? If yes, score high on explanatoriness; if no, score low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a practical scoring heuristic distilled from Steiner: explanatoriness should be assessed independently of correctness, elegance, or brevity by testing how the argument depends on and generalizes with the characterizing property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric design: score explanatoriness independently
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric for 'good proof' should score explanatoriness independently from rigor and beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanatoriness is a distinct dimension of quality; a correct/beautiful proof may still be non-explanatory. Provide a separate score or label for explanatory power in assessment rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric design: use the deformation test as a concrete check
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the deformation test as a concrete check in rubrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize explanatoriness by including an item that asks whether the proof generalizes under systematic variation of the key property and whether the proof suggests a family of related results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric design: reward proofs that suggest variants and generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reward proofs that suggest variants and generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give credit to arguments that naturally extend to related cases or expose parameters/structures one can vary to obtain new theorems; value this over isolated brute-force verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric design: distinguish structural from brute-force arguments
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should favor arguments that reveal organizing principles (symmetry, invariants, topology) over those that rely on ad-hoc calculations or generic tools that do not single out why the theorem holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric design: recognize context-dependence of what is 'characterizing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that what counts as 'characterizing' can be context-dependent and that the 'best' proof depends on what one wants to learn (verification vs. explanation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubrics should allow for different goals: sometimes verification suffices; other times explanation is desired. Be sensitive to prior knowledge and the intended explanatory target when judging explanatoriness.
